answers.justification: Haverlow's dispatch probes (C1) and the trailer telematics, which cannot be edited, (C6) show product at 2.4–3.5°C when the doors opened with no trend; Haverlow had 100% conformance in Q2 (C14); and night write-off rates are the same for Haverlow, Pellridge and own-label (C11), so the warm readings in E3 are not a supplier effect.

Night dock-to-chamber time rose from 44 min to 3 h 52 min, with pallets staged on an unrefrigerated dock at 15–17°C (C11), while chamber air stayed in spec (E6, C2); the lab found temperature abuse after manufacture (C3); and E3 receipt probes were keyed 2–4 h after the trailer doors closed (C6).

Chamber air held 1.7–3.9°C with alarms only in week 29 and no more than before (E6), the contractor visits found the plant within limits (C2), and the day-received lots going into the same chambers saw no rise in write-offs (C11).

The E3 probes were keyed at receipt confirmation (02:31–03:18), hours after the trailers were emptied (22:55–23:47, C6), when the trailer product probe had read 2.4–3.5°C, so the recorded receiving temperatures reflect dock dwell rather than condition off the trailer.

The self-certification change (C13) and the account manager's guess (E7) make over-claiming plausible, but genuine DC-caused spoilage also rose (C11, C4) and no claim-level data exists to tell the two apart.

Night dock-to-chamber time jumped in week 31, exactly when CR-2231 went live (E5, C11); night volume was unchanged (118 vs 121 pallets) and day shift was unchanged as a control (38→41 min); the mechanism is fewer operatives handling the same pallets.

Night write-off rates rose from 0.6% to 2.9%, equally across all suppliers, while day rates stayed at 0.5–0.6% into the same chambers (C11); the dock was 15–17°C; supplier and chamber rivals are ruled out (C6, E6, C2); and the lab confirms temperature abuse (C3).
Haverlow loads arrived at 2.4–3.6°C (C6, C1), and night write-off rates for Pellridge and own-label (2.8–2.9%) match Haverlow's 3.0% (C11), so arrival temperature does not explain the rise.

Corriebank credits rose from about £1,250 to £3,100 a week after self-certification began on 3 August (E7, C13), but the same period saw genuine DC-caused spoilage rise (C11, C4), and no claim-level breakdown separates the two causes.

The evidence clears Haverlow (C1, C6, C11), so A1 punishes the wrong party; it would also trigger capacity fees and 4–6% higher costs (C8, C15), the contractual notice and product-retention conditions appear unmet (C8), and the real cause would go unfixed.
It directly reverses the cause established in C11 and E5 (night receiving cut → dock dwell → write-offs) and adds weekly monitoring from WMS scan data, so the effect can be checked.
Over-claiming is still unestablished (E7 is a guess, and C11 and C4 show genuine spoilage rose), so asking Corriebank to change its terms on that basis would be committing before the evidence is in.

C13 lets Tallowmere request a claim-level extract, which would show whether the rise in customer credits is over-claiming or genuine spoilage from night-received lots; this is a sound secondary step but not the lead action.
It removes a protective receiving control (E3, C8) and does nothing about the real cause, which is the shortage of night staff (E5, C11).

For A2, there is a clear dose-response with a day-shift control (C11), the timing matches the change (E5), and the rivals are excluded (C6, E6, C2, C1); this is enough to commit to restoring night staffing, especially since monitoring is built in.

ambiguousItems: Q7 (R2): 'causal' vs 'association-only' — the evidence is a shift-level comparison with a strong control and rivals excluded, but there is no direct intervention.
Q9 (R4): 'association-only' vs 'unknown' — there is temporal coincidence, but the rise in genuine spoilage confounds it and there is no claim-level data.
Q5 (H5): 'unknown' vs weakly 'supported' — Corriebank credits rose faster (+148%) than the other customers' implied credits (~+74%), but there is no claim-level evidence.
caseProblems: C11's title ('dock-to-chamber times and DC-stage write-off rates by receiving shift') points strongly at the answer, and the item alone settles H2/R1/R2 and rules out H1/R3, so a single catalogue item does most of the discriminating work.
The E3 receipt times compared with the C6 door-closed times give a very clean mismatch of 2–4 hours; this is realistic but makes the H4 answer easy to read off once both are seen.

rulings.explanation: The answer semantics count a natural experiment, or temporal order plus mechanism plus covariation with the main rival ruled out, as enough for 'causal'. A direct intervention is not required. The case meets that bar. (1) CR-2231 (E5) is an exogenous change that hit night receiving only, with slots and volume unchanged (C11: 118 to 121 pallets). (2) C11 is a difference-in-differences. Night-received write-offs rose from 0.6% to 2.9%; day-received stayed at 0.5–0.6%. The comparison holds for the same suppliers (Pellridge, own-label) and the same chambers (CH1–CH3), which rules out the supplier and storage rivals. (3) The mechanism is shown directly. C6 puts product at 2.4–3.5°C at door-open. E3 records the same loads at 6.6–7.9°C at confirmation about 3.5 hours later, after dwell on 15–17°C unrefrigerated lanes (C11). C3 confirms a temperature-abuse spoilage profile. (4) The remaining rivals are excluded. C6 rules out arrival temperature and E6 rules out the chambers. Weather (C7) would hit day receiving too, and day receiving is the hotter period. C12 shows an unchanged reason-code mix, with 'damaged' at only 5%, so night handling damage is not the driver. A shift-level rather than pallet-level comparison does not undercut this: the only night-specific change runs through dock dwell, and the temperature trace ties the dwell to the warming. 'Association-only' would ignore the natural-experiment design that the semantics explicitly accept.

'Unknown' is reserved for evidence that is insufficient even to show association. Here E7 shows clear co-occurrence. The policy started on 3 August, and Corriebank credits rose from about £1,250 to about £3,100 a week over the same period. That rise is about £1,850 of the roughly £2,700 total credit rise in E1. So association is shown. Causation is not. Dock warming started in week 31, almost the same time, and E7 says Corriebank takes most of the night-only Haverlow lines. That gives Corriebank more exposure to dock-warmed product, so its faster rise (+148% against about +74% for other customers) is explained by genuine shelf-life loss as readily as by over-claiming. No claim-level data separates the two (C11 excludes credits; C13 only offers an extract). The confound stops 'causal' but does not remove the observed co-occurrence. That is exactly the 'association-only' category, so 'unknown' misreads the semantics.

'Supported' requires the evidence to favour H5 over its rivals. The only discriminating signal offered is the gap between Corriebank's credit growth (+148%) and other customers' (about +74%). E7 itself offers a full rival explanation: Corriebank takes most of the Haverlow lines, and all of them are night-received and dock-warmed (C11). A rough check shows the gap fits genuine spoilage. Night write-off rates rose about 4.8 times while day rates stayed flat. If credits track that, other customers' +74% implies roughly 19% night-received exposure and Corriebank's +148% implies roughly 39%. That is plausible for the customer taking most of the night-only supplier's lines. C4 gives no sign that Corriebank is out of line: 6 of 14 formal complaints against about 55% of sales, all citing genuine quality defects. E7's author says he has 'no hard evidence either way', and the key notes that no catalogue item tests whether claims are valid. The policy creates an opportunity, but nothing separates over-claiming from genuine loss. 'Unknown' (live but unestablished) is therefore the only defensible answer, and 'weakly supported' over-reads a confounded comparison.
